title: The gradient points uphill
summary: The gradient collects all partial derivatives into one vector. The slope in any unit direction u is ∇f · u, which is largest when u points along ∇f, so the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent, its length is that steepest slope, and it crosses contour lines at right angles. Gradient descent steps against it, with a step size set by the learning rate.
llm_link: Training a language model is gradient descent in a landscape with billions of dimensions: the height is the loss on a batch of text, and every step moves each weight a little against its own partial derivative, w ← w − η ∂L/∂w.
key_ideas: ∇f = [∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, …]: one partial per input, stacked into a vector.
Slope facing a unit direction û is ∇f · û. A dot product with a fixed arrow is largest along that arrow, so ∇f is the steepest uphill direction and |∇f| is the steepest slope.
Along a contour line the height is constant, so ∇f · û = 0: the gradient is perpendicular to the contours.
Gradient descent: repeat x ← x − η ∇f(x). In a long, narrow valley the steps zigzag.
The learning rate η sets the step size: too small crawls, too large overshoots and can climb.

quiz.q: For f(x, y) = x² + y², what is ∇f at (3, −1)?
quiz.explain: ∂f/∂x = 2x = 6 and ∂f/∂y = 2y = −2, so ∇f = [6, −2]. It points straight away from the bowl's centre, uphill.

quiz.q: Predict the result: ∇f = [3, 4] at a point. What is the slope facing the unit direction û = [0, 1]?
quiz.explain: Slope = ∇f · û = 3·0 + 4·1 = 4: facing straight along y you only feel ∂f/∂y.

quiz.q: With ∇f = [3, 4], what is the steepest possible slope at that point, and in which direction?
quiz.explain: The steepest direction is ∇f itself, scaled to length 1: [3, 4]/5 = [0.6, 0.8]. The slope there is |∇f| = 5.

quiz.q: Why is the gradient always perpendicular to the contour lines?
options: Because along a contour the height does not change, so ∇f · û = 0 for û along the contour
Because the gradient is always horizontal
It is only perpendicular at the minimum
quiz.explain: A zero dot product means a right angle, and walking along a contour has zero slope by definition.

quiz.q: A language-model training step uses w ← w − η·∂L/∂w with η = 0.001. If η were set to 10, what would most likely happen?
options: Steps would overshoot the valley and the loss would jump around or blow up
Nothing: η does not affect training
quiz.explain: The gradient only describes the landscape near the current weights. Huge steps leap past the valley floor and can land higher than before, so the loss diverges.

problems.title: The gradient of a bowl
problems.prompt:
For f(x, y) = x**2 + 3*y**2, write grad(x, y) that returns the gradient as a list [df/dx, df/dy].

Then write steepest(x, y) that returns the unit vector pointing uphill fastest: the gradient divided by its length. At the very bottom (gradient zero) there is no uphill, so raise ValueError.
problems.starter:
import math

def grad(x, y):
    # TODO: [2x, 6y]
    pass

def steepest(x, y):
    g = grad(x, y)
    # TODO 1: length = math.hypot(g[0], g[1]); if length == 0, raise ValueError("flat: no uphill direction")
    # TODO 2: return [g[0] / length, g[1] / length]
    pass

tests.name: gradient at (1, 1)
tests.code:
out = grad(1, 1)
assert out == [2, 6], f'∂/∂x of x² is 2x = 2, ∂/∂y of 3y² is 6y = 6; got {out}'

tests.name: gradient at (-2, 0.5)
tests.code:
out = grad(-2, 0.5)
assert out == [-4, 3], f'expected [2*(-2), 6*0.5] = [-4, 3], got {out}'

tests.name: steepest is a unit vector along the gradient
tests.code:
import math
out = steepest(3, 0)
assert out is not None, 'steepest returned None'
assert abs(out[0] - 1) < 1e-12 and abs(out[1]) < 1e-12, f'at (3, 0) the gradient is [6, 0], so uphill is [1, 0]; got {out}'
out = steepest(1, 1)
assert abs(math.hypot(*out) - 1) < 1e-12, f'the direction should have length 1, got {math.hypot(*out)}'

tests.name: flat bottom raises

hints: raise ValueError("...") is how to raise: ValueError is called like a function.

problems.title: Gradient descent on a bowl
problems.prompt:
Write descend(grad, start, lr, steps): start at the point start (a list), and steps times replace every coordinate p[i] with p[i] - lr * g[i], where g = grad(p). Return the list of all points visited, including the start (so steps + 1 points).

Then try different learning rates on f = x² + 6y² and watch the zigzag from the video.
problems.starter:
def descend(grad, start, lr, steps):
    p = list(start)
    path = [list(p)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        g = grad(p)
        # TODO: p = [p_i - lr * g_i for each coordinate]
        path.append(list(p))
    return path

tests.name: one step on x²
tests.code:
path = descend(lambda p: [2 * p[0]], [1.0], 0.1, 1)
assert len(path) == 2, f'1 step gives 2 points (start + 1), got {len(path)}'
assert abs(path[1][0] - 0.8) < 1e-12, f'x = 1 - 0.1 * 2 = 0.8, got {path[1][0]}. Did you step against the gradient (minus)?'

tests.name: reaches the bottom of the bowl
tests.code:
path = descend(lambda p: [2 * p[0], 12 * p[1]], [-5.2, 1.5], 0.05, 200)
x, y = path[-1]
assert abs(x) < 1e-6 and abs(y) < 1e-6, f'with a small learning rate the walk should end near (0, 0), got ({x:.4g}, {y:.4g})'

tests.name: zigzag in y with a bigger step
tests.code:
path = descend(lambda p: [2 * p[0], 12 * p[1]], [-5.2, 1.5], 0.15, 6)
ys = [q[1] for q in path]
signs = [y > 0 for y in ys]
assert all(signs[i] != signs[i + 1] for i in range(len(signs) - 1)), f'with lr = 0.15 the y coordinate should flip sign every step (zigzag), got {[round(y, 3) for y in ys]}'

tests.name: too large a step climbs
tests.code:
path = descend(lambda p: [2 * p[0]], [1.0], 1.1, 5)
assert abs(path[-1][0]) > abs(path[0][0]), f'with lr = 1.1 on x² every step overshoots and lands higher; got {[round(q[0], 3) for q in path]}'

hints: p = [pi - lr * gi for pi, gi in zip(p, g)]
Keep path.append(list(p)) after the update, so each new point is recorded.
problems.solution:
def descend(grad, start, lr, steps):
    p = list(start)
    path = [list(p)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        g = grad(p)
        p = [pi - lr * gi for pi, gi in zip(p, g)]
        path.append(list(p))
    return path

problems.title: Fit a line with gradient descent (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Put it together: fit y ≈ w*x + b by gradient descent on the mean squared error.

Write fit(x, y, lr=0.05, steps=2000) that starts at w = b = 0 and repeats:

err = w*x + b - y
dw = np.mean(2 * err * x)
db = np.mean(2 * err)
w, b = w - lr*dw, b - lr*db

Return (w, b) as floats.

tests.name: recovers a noiseless line
tests.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 21); y = 3 * x - 1
w, b = fit(x, y)
assert abs(w - 3) < 1e-3 and abs(b + 1) < 1e-3, f'the data is exactly y = 3x - 1, expected w ≈ 3, b ≈ -1; got w = {w:.4f}, b = {b:.4f}'

tests.name: agrees with least squares on noisy data
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = rng.uniform(-2, 2, 50); y = -0.5 * x + 2 + rng.normal(0, .2, 50)
w, b = fit(x, y)
W, B = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
assert abs(w - W) < 1e-3 and abs(b - B) < 1e-3, f'np.polyfit gives w = {W:.4f}, b = {B:.4f}; gradient descent gave w = {w:.4f}, b = {b:.4f}'

tests.name: returns floats
tests.code:
import numpy as np
w, b = fit(np.array([0., 1.]), np.array([1., 3.]), steps=10)
assert isinstance(w, float) and isinstance(b, float), f'return plain floats, got {type(w).__name__}, {type(b).__name__}'

hints: err is an array (one error per point); np.mean turns each slope into a single number.
Update both at once: w, b = w - lr * dw, b - lr * db
